In a reversible process, the heat absorbed is equal to TDSsys.

Now let’s apply Clausius’s inequality to processes occurring within an isolated system. In this case, there is no transfer of heat into or out of the system, and q 5 0. Therefore, for spontaneous processes within an isolated system, DS . 0.
The thermodynamic universe of a process (that is, a system plus its surround- ings) is clearly an isolated system to which Clausius’s inequality can be applied. It follows that

1. In a reversible process the total entropy of a system plus its surroundings is unchanged. 2. In an irreversible process the total entropy of a system plus its surroundings must increase. 3. A process for which DSuniv , 0 is not spontaneous.
These statements constitute the heart of the second law, because they justify its predictive power, which we stated as a postulate at the beginning of Section 13.5.
